1:1.t: Just as "in the last days" the Word of God, clothed with flesh from Mary, came forth into this world, and one thing indeed was that which was seen in him, another that which was understood — for the appearance of the flesh in him lay open to all, but the recognition of his divinity was granted to few and to the elect —, so also, when through the prophets or the lawgiver the Word of God is brought forth to men, it is not brought forth without fitting garments. For as there it is covered by the veil of the flesh, so here by the veil of the letter, so that the letter indeed is looked upon as flesh, but the spiritual sense lying hidden within is perceived as divinity. […]

1:2.t: The beginning, then, of Leviticus says that "the Lord called Moses and spoke to him from the tabernacle of testimony," that he might promulgate to the sons of Israel the laws of sacrifices and of offerings, and it says: "If a man offer an offering to God, let him offer from the oxen or the flock," that is, lambs or kids; "but if from the birds, turtledoves or young of doves." "But if" not a man, but "a soul offer an offering to God, from fine flour," it says, "let him offer unleavened loaves baked in the oven, or indeed fine flour from the pan sprinkled with oil, or from the griddle likewise kneaded in oil." […]

And first I should like to see what this distinction is: that of one it says that "a man" offers, of another that "a soul" offers, of another "the high priest", of another "the synagogue", of another "one soul from the people of the land". And I think indeed that "a man" is to be understood as one who, made "to the image and likeness" of God, lives rationally. This man, then, offers to God an offering — a "bull-calf", when he has overcome the pride of the flesh; a "sheep", when he has corrected the irrational and foolish motions; a "kid", when he has conquered wantonness. He offers too "a pair of turtledoves", when he has not been alone, but has joined his mind to the Word of God as to a true spouse, just as this kind of bird is said to keep a single and chaste marriage. […]

1:3.t: But if you wish to incline these things also to the moral level, you too have a "calf" which you ought to offer. Your flesh is a "calf," and indeed a very proud one; and if you wish to offer it as an offering to the Lord, so as to keep it chaste and modest, lead it "to the door of the tabernacle," that is, where it may be able to receive the hearing of the divine books. Let your offering be "male," let it not know woman, let it spurn concupiscence, let it flee frailty, let it seek nothing dissolute or soft. […]

1:4.t: And yet: "he shall lay his hand," it says, "upon the head of the victim, and they shall slaughter the calf before the Lord, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall offer the blood, and they shall pour out the blood at the altar round about, which is at the door of the tabernacle of testimony." It can indeed seem to have been said for this reason, that Annas and Caiaphas and the rest were of the sons of Aaron, "all who, taking counsel against Jesus, pronounced him guilty of death" and poured out his blood "around the base of the altar of the tabernacle of testimony." For there the blood is poured out where the altar and its base were, as the Lord himself also said: "because it does not befall a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem." […]

1:6.t: "And flaying," it says, "the whole burnt offering, they shall divide it limb by limb, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire upon the altar, and shall pile up wood on the fire; and the sons of Aaron the priest shall lay on the divided limbs and the head and the fat and the wood which are upon the altar. But the entrails and the feet they shall wash with water, and the priest shall lay all upon the altar; it is a victim and a sacrifice, an odor of sweetness to the Lord." How the flesh of the Word of God, which here is named a "calf," is flayed, and how it is divided "limb by limb" by the priests, is worth observing. […]

1:14.t: In very many ceremonies of the law one who needed to be cleansed was ordered to be cleansed by [offering] these [birds]. A pigeon indicates simplicity and a turtledove indicates chastity, for a pigeon is a lover of simplicity and a turtledove is a lover of chastity—so that if by chance one loses its mate it will not subsequently seek another.

2:1.t: But the offerings of the soul it describes as far inferior. This soul has neither a "bull-calf" nor a "sheep" nor a "kid" to offer to God; but it does not even find "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons". It has only "fine flour"; from it, it "offers unleavened loaves from the oven", from it a work made "in the pan" or "mixed with oil on the griddle". Whence it seems to me that the one here called "a soul" is to be understood as that man whom Paul names "the animal (natural) man"; who, even if he is not pressed by sins nor headlong toward vices, nevertheless does not have anything spiritual in him, anything that might figuratively be reckoned the flesh of the Word of God. […]

2:11.t: They quote the passage which says that "the lips of a strange woman drop as honeycomb," which is sweet indeed in the eater's mouth but is afterward found more bitter than gall. This, they argue, is the reason that neither honey nor wax is offered in the sacrifices of the Lord, and that oil, the product of the bitter olive, is burned in his temple.

2:13.t: For just as flesh, if it be not sprinkled with salt, however great and choice it be, is corrupted, so also the soul, unless it be in some way salted with continual temptations, immediately is dissolved and grows slack. Whence it is clear that on this account it was said that "every sacrifice shall be salted with salt."

Salt is good, and every offering must be sprinkled with it. Therefore also the apostle has given the commandment: "Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt." But "if the salt have lost his savor," it is cast out.

2:14.t: In the second place, the oblation "of the first fruits", that is, of the beginnings of the produce, is commanded. And this, if you remember well, the law commands to be done on the day of Pentecost. In which a "shadow" plainly was given to them, but for us the truth was reserved. For on the day of Pentecost, when the sacrifice of prayers had been offered, the Church received the first fruits of the coming "Holy Spirit" of the Apostles. And truly these were fresh, because it was new; whence they were even said to be "filled with new wine". "Roasted with fire". For fiery tongues settled upon each one. "And broken in the middle". For they were broken in the middle, when the letter was separated from the spirit. "And well cleansed". […]

There are four ways by which a sacrifice may be made acceptable. The sacrifice should consist of a gift, the newest of the new, or it should be dried or broken into pieces, or it should be unbroken. The "newest of the new" belongs to the early season of the year and is consistent with the nature of first-fruits. Now, it has been made clear to us that this refers to those who are renewed by the sacrament of baptism. That, in fact, is the real sacrifice of first-fruits when a person offers himself as a victim and begins of himself to act so as to ensure in the future an offering of a gift that is his very own. The new faith of those who have been made new is strong and vigorous, seeking for itself an increase of virtue. […]
2:14.s: On Cain and Abel, Book 2, Chapter 6

3:1.t: After this it speaks of the peace (salutary) offerings, which are offered from animals, that is, from "oxen" or "goats and sheep"; and nothing beyond these is admitted for immolation — not even the birds, which above had been admitted among the offerings to be offered. For this one, who offers the peace offerings, is without doubt already conscious of his own salvation; and therefore he who has arrived at salvation must of necessity offer things that are great and perfect. For thus the Apostle too says: "solid food, however, is for the perfect".

He says clearly that the blood of the victims slain is a propitiation in the place of human life. And the law about sacrifices suggests that it should be so regarded, if it is carefully considered. For it requires him who is sacrificing always to lay his hands on the head of the victim, and to bear the animal to the priest held by its head, as one offering a sacrifice on behalf of himself. Thus he says in each case:

"He shall bring it before the Lord. And he shall lay his hands on the head of the gift."

Such is the ritual in every case, no sacrifice is ever brought up otherwise. And so the argument holds that the victims are brought in place of the lives of them who bring them.
3:1.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 10

3:9.t: And by the precept of the law, the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered in sacrifice. In the tail, of course, is the end of the body; and he sacrifices well who brings the sacrifice of a good work to the end of the required action.

4:2.t: Thereupon the order of the sacrifices is directed to the offering of victims for sins, in which it is said a second time: "the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: whatever soul shall sin before the Lord unwillingly". Rightly does it say "soul" of the one whom it describes as sinning; for it would not have called it spirit, of which it would say that it would sin; but neither would it call this one a man, in whom, with sin intervening, the "image of God" in no way stands firm. It is not, then, the spirit that sins; for "the fruit of the spirit" — as the Apostle describes — "is love, joy, peace, patience", and the rest like these, which are also called "the fruits of life". Finally, elsewhere too he says: "he who sows in the flesh shall from the flesh reap corruption; […]

4:3.t: The discourse concerns the sacrifices which are offered by those who have sinned through ignorance or not by will. Hence also in what went before, when we were speaking of the high priest's sacrifice, we observed that it was not written of him that he had been in ignorance. But if anyone remembers well the things that were said, he can say to us that the sacrifice which we said the high priest offered "for sin" we set down as holding the figure of Christ. And it will not seem fitting that Christ, "who knew no sin", should be said to have offered a sacrifice "for sin", even though the matter is transacted through a mystery and the same one is set down both as high priest and as victim. […]

For "on account of sins not voluntary" it is in general the "soul" that is commanded to offer, but after this the text proceeds through diverse and various persons; and it is commanded that, "if indeed it be the high priest who has transgressed and offers a sacrifice for sin, he should offer a bull-calf" as a whole burnt offering, but not by that same rite by which he offered the one for an offering. For of this one he shall place upon the altar of the whole burnt offerings "the fat and the two kidneys with their fat, and the fat that covers the inner parts", only these. "Of its blood" too, "dipping his finger, he sprinkles seven times before the Lord, and anoints from it the horns of the altar of incense. […]

But these things have been said in general; now, however, they are divided by kinds. "If the high priest", it says, "who has been anointed, should sin, so as to make the people sin, he shall offer for his own sin a bull-calf from the oxen, without blemish, to the Lord". Both terror and mercy are displayed together in the divine laws. Is nothing, then, after all, safe — not even the high priest? And what high priest? The very one who has been anointed, the very one who kindles the divine altars with the sacred fires, who immolates offerings and peace offerings to God; who intervenes as a certain mediating re-propitiator between God and men — not even he, I say, remains immune from the contagion of sin. But see the mercy of God, and know it more fully from Paul's teaching. […]

But in the moral sense this high priest can be seen as that faculty of piety and religion which within us performs, as it were, a certain priesthood, through the prayers and supplications that we pour out to God. If this transgress in anything, it forthwith "makes sin" the whole people of good acts that is within us. For we do nothing of a right work when the guiding sense of good works has declined into what is depraved; and therefore for the amending of this, not any victim whatever, but the sacrifice of "the fatted calf" itself is required. Likewise too the fault of the synagogue — that is, the amending of all the virtues that are within us — is repaired not otherwise than by the mortification of Christ.

4:5.t:
Moses was the first to make known the name of Christ as a name especially august and glorious. When he delivered types and symbols of heavenly things, and mysterious images, in accordance with the oracle which said to him, "Look that thou make all things according to the pattern which was shown thee in the mount," he consecrated a man high priest of God, in so far as that was possible, and him he called Christ. And thus to this dignity of the high priesthood, which in his opinion surpassed the most honorable position among men, he attached for the sake of honor and glory the name of Christ.

He knew so well that in Christ was something divine. […]

He is called by two names, Jesus Christ; Jesus because he is a savior, Christ because he is a priest. With this in mind the divinely inspired prophet Moses gave these two titles to two men eminent above all, changing the name of his own successor in the sovereignty, Auses, to Jesus, and giving his own brother, Aaron, the surname Christ, that through these two chosen men he might represent at once the high priesthood and the kingship of the one Jesus Christ who was to come.

4:6.t: It will now be a great task to pursue the diversities of victims and the rites and varieties of sacrifices, and one belonging to a work far other than that discourse which the common crowd receives in the general assembly. But that we may seem to touch upon some things in passing: almost every victim, indeed, which is offered has something of the form and image of Christ. For every victim is recapitulated in him, so much so that, after "he himself was offered", all the victims ceased which had preceded him in type and "shadow"; concerning which, as far as we could, we showed in what went before how the bull-calf offered by the high priest, whether as an offering or "for sin", held his form. […]

4:13.t: But if there be a sin "of the whole synagogue", the synagogue is none the less commanded to offer "a bull-calf" as a whole burnt offering. But in the sin of the synagogue it is said: "if it should be ignorant, and the matter be hidden from the eyes of the synagogue, and it should do one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done"; from which it is clear that "the whole synagogue" too can transgress through ignorance. And this the Lord also confirms in the gospels, when he says: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do".

4:22.t: "But if a ruler", it says, "should sin, he shall offer a goat from the she-goats". This ruler can be seen as the power of reason which is within us. And if this should sin in us, and we should do something foolish, that sentence of the Savior is to be greatly feared by us, which says: "you are the salt of the earth. But if the salt should lose its savor, it is good for nothing, except to be cast out and trodden underfoot by men". This one too, then, has his own victim.

4:27.t: But "one soul", it says, "if it should sin, shall likewise offer a female goat", according to that substitution of victims which we mentioned above. But perhaps the hearers of the church may say: it was dealt with almost better among the ancients than with us, when, sacrifices being offered by diverse rites, pardon was granted to those who sinned. Among us there is only one pardon of sins, which is given at the beginning through the grace of the laver; after this no mercy is granted to the one who sins, nor any pardon. It befits indeed a Christian, "for whom Christ died", to be of stricter discipline. For them sheep, goats, oxen were slaughtered, and birds, and fine flour was sprinkled; for you the Son of God was slaughtered, and does it delight you to sin again? […]

But let us see what is also to be thought concerning the things that have just now been read: "but if", it says, "one soul should sin unwillingly from the people of the land, by doing one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done, and should transgress, and the sin which it sinned should become known to it, it shall bring its gift: it shall bring a female goat from the kids, without blemish, for the sin which it sinned". And after this it recounted the whole rite of the sacrifice, according to what we expounded above. Concerning the soul which, made under sin, it says offers, how it is to be thought, we have explained in the foregoing as far as we could; […]

Consider, again, other instances of the impossibility of all men following the law of Moses. He makes a distinction between voluntary transgressions and those hard to evade, and after assigning penalties to sins which deserve the severest punishment, he provides laws by which those who sin unwittingly are to receive different treatment. One of these runs as follows:

"27. And if a soul of the people of the land shall sin unwittingly by doing anything contrary to the commandments of the Lord that ought not to be done, and shall transgress, 28. and his sin shall be known to him, wherein he hath sinned [in it], then shall he bring [his gift] a kid of the goats, a female without blemish, he shall bring it for his sin that he hath sinned 29. […]
4:27.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 1, Chapter 3

5:1.t: But let us now see what that soul also does which "hears the voice of one swearing an oath and is a witness", "or" which "sees" something "and is privy to it and does not disclose it", from which it too "has borne his sin" — without doubt his who either did something wickedly or swore. This also, according to the history, builds us up and teaches us never to pollute our consciences in another's sins, nor to lend consent to those who act wickedly. And I call it consent not only to act along with them, but also to keep silent about the things that have been done unlawfully. Do you wish to know that these things agree also with the Gospel precepts? The Lord himself says: "if you see your brother sin, reprove him between yourself and him alone. […]

5:2.t: After these things another law is promulgated. "Whatever soul", it says, "touches any unclean thing, or the carcass of unclean beasts, and it is hidden from him, and he is defiled; or if he touches of the uncleanness of a man, of any uncleanness by which he may be defiled", and so forth. These things indeed are observed among the Jews quite unbecomingly and uselessly. For to what end is he held unclean who has touched, for example, a dead animal or the body of a deceased man? What if it be the body of a prophet? What if the body of a patriarch, or even of Abraham himself? What if he has touched even the bones, will he be unclean? What if he touches the bones of Elisha, which raise up the dead? […]

5:4.t: Now a third law of this kind is promulgated: "and the soul", it says, "which swears, pronouncing with its lips to do evil or to do good, according to all things whatsoever he shall utter to a man with an oath, and it is hidden from him, and afterward he knows it, and has sinned in some one of these — let him pronounce the sin which he has sinned, and he shall bring for the things in which he has offended, to the Lord, for the sin by which he has sinned, a female of the sheep" and so forth. How indeed, "if I pronounce with my lips or swear to do good" and do not do it, I am guilty of sin, there is no difficulty in showing; but how, "if I swear or pronounce to do evil" and do not do it, I have sinned, it is difficult to assign in word. […]

5:7.t: Through Moses God orders that two young birds, a pair of pigeons or of turtledoves, be offered for any sin. This means that the sinlessness of such gentle birds and their guilelessness and forgetfulness of injury is very acceptable to God. So he is instructing us to offer a sacrifice bearing the character of that against which we have offended. The plight of the poor doves, moreover, will instill into us a beginning of abhorrence for sin.

Not without cause is a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons, taken in the sacrifices: for they are of equal worth, and it is never said separately, a pair only of pigeons, but a pair of turtledoves, and two young pigeons. The dove is the Holy Spirit. But the Holy Spirit, when he speaks of great and more hidden mysteries, which many cannot receive, is signified by the name of the turtledove — that is, of that bird which dwells always on the ridges of the mountains and on the tops of the trees; but in the valleys, and in the things which reach even to men, the dove is taken.
5:7.s: HOMILIES ON THE SONG OF SONGS, HOMILY 2

5:15.t: But what shall we say concerning the sacrifice of the "ram" bought "at a price" and "at the price of a shekel of the sanctuary", which is commanded to be offered for the expiation of sin? He is going to be rich who can purge his offenses "at the price of a ram". What these riches are, let us seek. The most wise Solomon teaches us, saying: "the redemption of a man's soul is his own proper riches". Do you hear the words of wisdom, how with necessary properties it declares the force of each word? He speaks of riches suited to "the redemption of the soul", and riches not another's nor common, but "proper riches". By which he shows that there are certain "proper riches" and certain riches not proper. […]

Let us now see what law is set forth in offering victims "for sin". "And the Lord spoke", it says, "to Moses, saying: if any soul is hidden and sins unwillingly against the holy things of the Lord, he shall offer for his offense to the Lord a spotless ram of the sheep, at the price of a silver shekel of the sanctuary, for that in which he offended. And what he has sinned against the holy things, he shall restore, and shall add a fifth to it, and shall give it to the priest; and the priest shall make entreaty for him with the ram of the offense, and it shall be forgiven him". […]

5:16.t: But let us too, to whom these things perhaps do not happen, see in what part the discourse of the law may build us up. And I today, though I am a sinner, yet because the dispensation of the Lord's word has been entrusted to me, seem to have the holy things of God committed to me. Nor now for the first time, but often already and long since, do we use this dispensation toward you. If, therefore, anyone of you has received from me the Lord's money and, as is wont to happen, having gone out of the church and been snatched away by the various occupations of the world, has given to oblivion the things he had heard, and has fulfilled no work from the word which he received, this is he who has not restored the money received from the holy things. […]

6:2.t: If, according to the faith of the divine law, these things which are read to us were spoken by the Lord to Moses, I think that, as being the words of God, they ought to be understood not according to the incapacity of the hearers but according to the majesty of the one speaking. "The Lord," it says, "spoke." What is "the Lord"? Let the Apostle answer you, and learn from him that "the Lord is spirit." But if the word of the Apostle does not suffice for you, hear the Lord himself saying in the Gospels that "God is spirit." If therefore both the Lord and God is "spirit," the things which the spirit speaks we ought to hear spiritually. But I say yet something more: that the things the Lord speaks are to be believed not only spiritual, but even spirit. […]

Let us therefore now see what is the "deposit" which each of the faithful has received. I think that we have received both our own soul and our body as a deposit from God. And do you wish to see another, greater "deposit" which you have received from God? To your very soul God entrusted "his own image and likeness." This deposit, therefore, must be restored by you as whole as it is established to have been received by you. For if you are merciful, "as your Father in heaven is merciful," the image of God is in you and you preserve the "deposit" whole. If you are perfect, "as your Father also in heaven is perfect," the deposit of the image of God remains in you. […]

Let us now see what also is to be understood by "partnership." Do you suppose there is anyone who ought to be admonished according to the letter, lest perchance in a matter of money, or in any other kind of partnership, he deceive his partner by fraud? Of the utmost misery is that soul into which this kind of fraud can still fall. Yet nevertheless, because there is much fragility in man, let us admonish concerning these things also, since not even the Apostle was reluctant to command them. For he says: "let no one overreach his brother in business, since God is the avenger of all these things." But now let us inquire what also is the "partnership of the spirit." […]

6:3.t: Then the lawgiver adds: "or if he has done any harm to his neighbor, or if he has found something lost." The law of the letter seems to command this, that, if anyone finds what another has lost and it is asked for, he restore it and let it "not perish for him." This too is a useful edification for the hearers. For many think it is without sin if they retain another's property which they have found, and they say: God gave it to me, to whom do I have to render it? Let them learn, therefore, that this sin is like robbery, if anyone does not return what he has found. Yet nevertheless, if the lawgiver had wished only this, which is thought according to the letter, to be understood, he could have said: if he finds what had perished, or what someone had lost. […]

For if Christ took away from us that very heavy yoke of many observances, so that we are not circumcised according to the flesh, we do not immolate victims of the cattle, we do not rest even from necessary works on the Sabbath, retaining the seventh in the revolution of the days, and other things of this kind; but keep them as spiritually understood, and, the symbolizing shadows being removed, are watchful in the light of those things which are signified by them; shall we therefore say, that when it is written that whoever finds another man's property of any kind that has been lost, should return it to him who has lost it, it does not pertain to us? and many other like things whereby people learn to live piously and uprightly? […]
6:3.s: AGAINST TWO LETTERS OF THE PELAGIANS 3.10

6:5.t: Both this one, who "found perdition," and that one who found "robbery," and also he who "denied the deposit," and everyone whosoever in any part "has harmed the soul of his neighbor and has sworn unjustly": "he shall restore," it says, "the principal itself and shall add a fifth part over and above, and to him whose it is he shall render it," according, at least, to that exposition concerning the adding of the fifth parts which we have already given before. "And he shall offer," it says, "to the Lord a ram of the sheep without blemish, at a price, for that in which he offended; and the priest shall pray for him before the Lord, and it shall be remitted him for the one of all the things which he did and offended in it." […]

Some think that the precepts of the Old Testament are stricter than those of the New; but these are certainly deceived by careless consideration. For in the Old Testament, not avarice but robbery is punished. There, property unjustly taken is punished by fourfold restitution. But here this rich man is not blamed for taking what belonged to others, but for not giving what was his own.

6:8.t: After these things it follows: "and the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: command Aaron and his sons, saying: this is the law of the whole burnt offering. This whole burnt offering shall be in its burning upon the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn upon it and shall not be extinguished. And the priest shall put on himself the linen tunic, and shall put on the linen undergarment about his body, and shall take away the victim which the fire has consumed, the whole burnt offering, from the altar, and shall place it beside the altar. And he shall strip himself of his robe and be clothed with another robe, and shall cast out the victim which has been burned outside the camp into a clean place. […]

6:9.t: A holocaust is burned on the altar when a good work is performed with the burning fire of charity in the heart of any elect person who is devoted to God completely (that is, with both body and soul). This is done all night until the morning when one does not cease to persevere in good works throughout all the time of his life, until one is taken from the body and merits seeing the morning of the world to come. The fire will be on the same altar, because we ought to be burning with that charity alone which the Lord gives to his church through the Holy Spirit.

6:10.t: The priest who offers the holocaust is the Lord who is himself accustomed to kindle in us the fire of his charity and through it to make the sacrifices of our good actions acceptable to himself. And he is clothed in linen garments when he does these things because, in order that he may excite us to works of virtue, he sets before us the examples of his own incarnation, passion and death, which can be signified by linen, as we have frequently said.

6:14.t: After this: "this is," it says, "the law of the sacrifice which the sons of Aaron the priest shall offer before the altar in the presence of the Lord. He shall take from it a full hand of the fine flour of the sacrifice with its oil and with all its frankincense, which are for the sacrifice, and shall place upon the altar the victim, an odor of sweetness, its memorial to the Lord. But what remains of it, Aaron and his sons shall eat. Unleavened it shall be eaten in a holy place; in the court of the tabernacle of testimony they shall eat it. It shall not be cooked leavened; this portion I have given to them from the offerings of the Lord; they are a holy of holies, as is that for sin and for offense. All the males of the priests shall eat it; […]

Therefore the sacrifice, for which all these sacrifices had gone before in type and figure, one and perfect — "Christ" has been "immolated." If anyone "touches" the flesh of this sacrifice, he is immediately "sanctified"; if he is unclean, he is healed, if he is under a "plague." Thus at last did she understand — she of whom I made mention a little before, "who was suffering an issue of blood" — that he himself was the flesh of the sacrifice and the flesh of the "holy of holies"; and because she truly understood what was the flesh of the "holy of holies," for this reason she drew near. […]

6:15.t: And well is it that the things which are offered from the sacrifice of fine flour are offered "with a full hand, with oil" and "frankincense, for an odor of sweetness to the Lord." This passage the Apostle Paul briefly explained to the Philippians, saying: "I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odor of sweetness, a victim accepted, pleasing to God." In which he shows that mercy toward the poor pours oil into the sacrifice of God, but the ministry which is rendered to the saints puts on the sweetness of frankincense. But this is commanded to be done "with a full hand." For thus the same Apostle says, that "he who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; but he who sows in blessing shall also reap of blessing." […]

6:19.t: It is added in what follows: "and the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: this is the offering of Aaron and of his sons, which they shall offer to the Lord on the day when you shall anoint him, the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour in sacrifice always, half of it in the morning, and half of it after noon. In a pan it shall be made with oil, sprinkled he shall offer it soft, a sacrifice of fragments, a sacrifice for an odor of sweetness to the Lord. The priest who shall be anointed in his stead from among his sons shall make them; an eternal law; all shall be consummated. And every sacrifice of a priest shall be a whole burnt offering, and shall not be eaten." In the other precepts indeed the high priest furnishes his office to the people in offering the sacrifices; […]

6:25.t: But let us now see what those things are which are set forth in the law. "And the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the law of the sin offering" and the rest which have been read in the present passage. And I remember that we have already said before that the law is not always given to the same persons, but one thing indeed is said to the sons of Israel, another to the sons of Aaron, and yet another, as we observed some time ago, to Moses and Aaron. There is also another law which is given to Moses alone, so that not even Aaron is made a partaker of that law. Who has been so illumined by God with the gift of knowledge as to be able to discourse fully and clearly on the distinctions and diversities of each of these? […]

But concerning these things, so far as we were able, we have explained in the foregoing; now, however, we add this, that it says: "in the place in which the whole burnt offerings are slaughtered, there also the victims for sin". See how great is the mercy and kindness of God, that where the "whole burnt offering" is slaughtered — that which is offered to God alone — there also the "victim" which is "for sin" is commanded to be immolated; so that, namely, he who has sinned and repents, "being turned to God", and slays the victim of "a contrite spirit", may understand that he now stands in a "holy place" and is joined to those things which pertain to God. There, then, is the "victim for sin" immolated, where also the "whole burnt offering": "in the sight," it says, "of the Lord". […]

"And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying: This is the law of the sin offering; in the place where the whole burnt offerings are slaughtered, they shall also slay that which is for sin before the Lord; they are the holy of holies. The priest who offers it shall eat it; it shall be eaten in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle of testimony. Everyone who touches its flesh shall be sanctified; and whoever has been sprinkled with its blood upon a garment, whatever has been sprinkled, that too shall be washed in a holy place. And the earthen vessel in which it has been cooked shall be broken; but if it has been cooked in a bronze vessel, he shall scour it and rinse it with water. Every male of the priests shall eat of these; […]

7:1.t: "And this is," it says, "the law of the ram which is for the trespass; the holy of holies. In the place in which they slaughter the whole burnt offerings, they shall also slaughter the ram which is for the trespass, before the Lord" and so forth. In the divine Scriptures it seems that frequently sin is named for trespass and trespass for sin indifferently and without any distinction; in this passage, however, it is found to be distinguished. For when above, in the victim "for sin", it had delivered the rite and order of the sacrifice, now it separately enjoins a sacrifice "for the trespass"; and although all things are enjoined in the same order and with the same observance, and it adds at the very end: "as that which is for sin, so also that which is for trespass; […]

7:9.t: "And every sacrifice which is made in the oven, and everything which is made on the gridiron or in the frying-pan, shall be the priest's who offers it; it shall be his". What do we say? Are we to suppose that almighty God, who gave responses to Moses from heaven, gave precepts about the "oven" and the "gridiron" and the "frying-pan", so that the people might learn through Moses that through these God would become propitious to them, if they fried certain things "in the frying-pan", cooked certain things "in the oven", roasted certain things "on the gridiron"? But "not so" did the children of the Church "learn Christ", nor were they "instructed in him" through the Apostles in such a way, that they should suppose anything so lowly and so cheap concerning "the Lord of majesty". […]

7:10.t: After these things: "and every sacrifice," it says, "made in oil or not made shall belong to all the sons of Aaron, to each equally". What sacrifice is "made in oil" or which is that "not made in oil"? The "sacrifice of the peace offering" is commanded to be made "in oil", as we have already said above. But the "sacrifice for sin" is not made "in oil"; for it says: "he shall not put oil upon it, since it is for sin". That, then, which is "for sin", neither is the "oil of gladness" put upon it nor the incense of sweetness; for concerning those who sin the Apostle says: "and I shall mourn those who have sinned before and have not done penance". Nor is there in it the "odor of sweetness", because from the person of the sinner it is said: "my scars have rotted and are corrupted". […]

7:11.t: "This is," it says, "the law of the sacrifice of the peace offering, which they shall offer to the Lord. If indeed he offers it for a thanksgiving, he shall also bring to the sacrifice loaves of thanksgiving made of fine flour in oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, and fine meal mingled with oil. Upon leavened loaves he shall offer his gifts, because it is the sacrifice of thanksgiving of his peace offering. And he shall offer of it one from all his gifts as a separation to the Lord; it shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the peace offering; and the flesh of the sacrifice of thanksgiving of the peace offering, it shall be his; and on the day on which the gift is offered, they shall eat it, and they shall not leave any of it until the morning". […]

7:15.t: But as to what it says: "it shall be eaten within the day, nor shall it be left over of it until the morning", let us compare it with the other sacrifices and let us see what the reason is that in this peace sacrifice indeed it commanded "the things that are offered" to be "eaten on the same day", but in another sacrifice it allows them to be kept even to the second day and up to the third, but on the third day the things that remain over to be already delivered to the fire, lest they defile the one who offers. What, then, this difference may hold, let us see. […]

7:16.t: It is said, then, in what follows: "but if it be a vow, or if he sacrifice his gift voluntarily, on whatever day he shall have offered his sacrifice, it shall be eaten, and on the following day. And what remains over of the flesh of the sacrifice until the third day shall be burned with fire. But if by eating anyone eats of the flesh on the third day, it shall not be accepted from him who offers it, it shall not be reckoned to him, it is a defilement. And whatever soul eats of it shall bear the sin". This is doubtless what David too says in the Psalms: "let his prayer become sin", when not only nothing of merit, but even much of guilt is sought from the sacrifices. […]

7:19.t: "And any flesh that has been touched by anything unclean shall not be eaten, it shall be burned with fire. Everyone who is clean shall eat the flesh; and whatever soul eats the flesh of the sacrifice of the peace offering, which is the Lord's, and his uncleanness is in him, that soul shall perish from his people. And whatever soul touches any unclean thing, whether from the uncleanness of a man or of unclean quadrupeds or from any unclean abomination, and eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of the peace offering, which is the Lord's, that soul shall perish from his people". The lawgiver here has set forth threefold causes of uncleanness. One, that the "flesh" of the sacrifices not be touched by any "uncleanness". […]

7:23.t: "And the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: You shall not eat any fat of oxen and of sheep and of goats. And the fat of carrion, and of what is caught from a wild beast, shall not be for any work, and shall not be eaten as food. Everyone who eats the fat of the cattle from which you offer from them a victim to the Lord, that soul shall perish from his people. And you shall not eat any blood in all your habitation, from cattle and from birds. Every soul, whatever it be, that eats blood, that soul shall perish from his people". The lawgiver refuses that the "fats" of those animals which are offered in the sacrifices, and of certain others, be eaten or held in use; but he forbids the "blood" of any flesh to be eaten. […]

7:28.t: After these things: "and the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: And speak to the sons of Israel, saying: He who offers a sacrifice of his peace offering to the Lord shall offer his gift to the Lord from the sacrifice of his peace offering. His hands shall offer the victim to the Lord: the fat which is upon the little breast and the lobe of the liver, he shall offer them so that they be set as a gift before the Lord. And the priest shall place the fat which is upon the little breast upon the altar, and the little breast shall be Aaron's and his sons'. And the right arm you shall give as a separation to the priest from your peace offerings. He who offers the blood of the peace offering and the fat from the sons of Aaron, to him shall the right arm be as a portion. […]

7:35.t: The Apostle briefly shows the reason why these things that are read to us can be understood or not understood, saying that from his eyes "the veil of the old testament can be taken away, whoever shall have turned to the Lord"; from which he wished it to be known that, the less these things are plain to us, the less is our conversion to God. And therefore we must strive with all our strength that, being free from the occupations of the world and from worldly affairs, and leaving behind even those superfluous tales of our companions, if it can be done, we may give our effort to the word of God and "meditate on his law day and night", so that, being converted with our whole heart, we may be able to behold the unveiled and open face of Moses, and especially in these things which have […]

8:1.t: Let us see, then, in what order the high priest is appointed. "Moses," he says, "gathered together the congregation, and says to them: This is the word which the Lord commanded." Although, therefore, the Lord had commanded concerning the appointing of the high priest and the Lord had chosen him, nevertheless the congregation too is gathered together. For in the ordination of a priest there is required also the presence of the people, so that all may know and be assured that the one who is more excellent out of all the people, who is more learned, who is more holy, who is more eminent in every virtue, that one is chosen for the priesthood, and this with the people standing by, lest afterward any reconsideration should arise for anyone, lest any scruple should remain. […]

8:3.t: Well is the church named ecclesia ["assembly"], because it calls forth and assembles all men, as the Lord says in Leviticus: "Then assemble the whole community at the entrance of the meeting tent." It is worthy of note that this word assemble is used in the Scriptures for the first time in the passage when the Lord established Aaron in the high priesthood. In Deuteronomy God says to Moses, "Assemble the people for me; I will have them hear my words, that they may learn to fear me." He mentions the name of the church again when he says of the tablets: "And on them were inscribed all the words that the Lord spoke to you on the mountain from the midst of the fire on the day of the assembly"; as if he would say more plainly, "on the day on which you were called and gathered together." […]

8:6.t: With attentive ears and watchful heart hear the consecration of the high priest, or of the priest, because you too, according to the promises of God, are priests of the Lord: "for you are a holy nation and a priesthood." Moses, he says, took according to the command of the Lord "Aaron and his sons", and first indeed he washes them, and afterward he clothes them. Consider more carefully the order of the words: first he washes, afterward he clothes. For you cannot be clothed unless you have first been washed. "Wash yourselves," therefore, "and be clean, and take away your wickednesses from your souls." […]

8:7.t: So then he washed him and clothed him. With what garment? "With a tunic," he says, "and he girded him with the girdle, and again he clothed him with the ankle-length tunic", or, as we read elsewhere, "the inner tunic". With two tunics, as I see, the high priest is clothed through Moses. But what do we make of the fact that Jesus forbade his priests, our Apostles, to use two tunics? And we had said that Moses and Jesus, that is, the law and the gospels, are consonant with one another. […]

8:8.t: "And he girded him," he says, "according to the making of the ephod." Already above too he had said that "he girded him with the girdle" over the tunic, and now again he is girded "according to the making of the ephod". What is this double girdle, with which he wishes the high priest to be bound fast on every side? Let him be bound fast in word, bound fast in work, ready for all things, nothing slack, let him have nothing loose. Let him be girded with the virtues of the soul, let him be bound fast from bodily vices, let him fear no lapse of the soul, none of the body, let him always use both girdles, "that he may be chaste in body and spirit". And well is it that he is girded also "according to the making of the ephod". […]

8:9.t: But he has not yet finished, and yet another ornament is to be added; it is necessary that he receive also a crown. Therefore he receives first the "cidaris", which is either a certain covering of the head or an ornament. And after these things there is set upon him the "mitre". "Before the face", that is, from the forehead of the high priest, "the golden plate, hallowed", on which the name of God is said to be engraved. Truly this ornament of the head, where the name of God is said to be placed, is set on above all those things with which the lower members of the body had been adorned. […]

8:12.t: You must know that this chrism [chrismation] is prefigured in the Old Testament. When Moses, conferring on his brother the divine appointment, was ordering him high priest, he anointed him after he had bathed in water, and thenceforward he was called "christ" ["anointed"], clearly after the figurative Chrism.

8:13.t: But as for what he says: "And Moses brought near the sons of Aaron, and clothed them with tunics and girded them with girdles and put upon them cidaras, as the Lord commanded Moses", it must be attended to what is the difference of the lesser priests to the greater priesthoods. To these neither are double vestments handed over, nor the "ephod", nor the "rational", nor the "ornament of the head", but only the "cidaris" and the "girdles", which bind the tunic. These too, then, receive the grace of the priesthood, and these too discharge the office, but not as that one who is adorned both with the "ephod" and the "rational", who is resplendent "with manifestation and truth", who is decorated with the ornament of the "golden plate". […]

9:7.t: It seems that they have not paid sufficient attention to the fact that Zachary was a priest and that all priests at that time were obliged by the law of God to offer sacrifice first for their own sins and then for those of the people. Therefore, as it is now proved by the sacrifice of prayer that we are not sinless, since we are [daily] commanded to say, "Forgive us our debts," so it was proved then by the sacrifice of animal victims that the priests were not sinless, since they were commanded to offer the victim for their own sins.

10:1.t: The sons of Aaron also, who set upon the altar a strange fire not commanded by the Lord, were at once blotted out in the sight of the avenging Lord. These examples, you will see, are being followed wherever the tradition which comes from God is despised by lovers of strange doctrine and replaced by teaching of merely human authority.
10:1.s: Treatise I. On the Unity of the Church 18-19

10:1.t: Nor do we propose this, dearest brother, without the authority of divine Scripture, when we say that all things are arranged by divine direction by a certain law and by special ordinance, and that none can usurp to himself, in opposition to the bishops and priests, anything which is not of his own right and power. For Korah, Dathan, and Abiram endeavoured to usurp, in opposition to Moses and Aaron the priest, the power of sacrificing; and they did not do without punishment what they unlawfully dared. The sons of Aaron also, who placed strange fire upon the altar, were at once consumed in the sight of an angry Lord; […]

The work of a man who has murmured or has been detected in pride must not be mixed with that done by men humble in heart and of a contrite spirit; it must not be used at all by the pious. “For that which is exalted among men is an abomination before God.” And there is another command of the apostle: “Neither murmur ye, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer.” Then there is this: “Not grudgingly or of necessity.” So the work of such men is unacceptable, like a blemished sacrifice—which it was impious to mingle with the offerings of other men. For if those who brought strange fire to the altar experienced such great wrath, surely it is perilous to accept a work springing from a mind hostile to God to assist us in keeping God’s commandments.

I hear again that Nadab and Abihu, for having merely offered incense with strange fire, were with strange fire destroyed, the instrument of their impiety being used for their punishment, and their destruction following at the very time and place of their sacrilege; and not even their father Aaron, who was next to Moses in the favor of God, could save them.

So it was also when Abihu and Nadab, men of priestly blood, were consumed by fire from heaven, in whose case, to be sure, the Lord wished to show not merely judgment but judgment immediately impending. For it is written that when the fire sent by the Lord had consumed the burnt offering: "Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took either of them his censer, and put fire therein and put incense thereon, and offered strange fire before the Lord, which he commanded them not. And there went out fire from the Lord and devoured them and they died before the Lord." What else did he wish than to show his right hand stretched over us, and his sword ever threatening? […]
10:1.s: On the Government of God, Book 1, Chapter 11

10:1.t: This is not far from being a sign of our unhappy time, in which some who have attained positions as priests and teachers—merely to mention it is both distressing and sad enough—are consumed by the fire of heavenly vengeance because they prefer the fire of cupidity to the fire of heavenly love. Their eternal damnation was prefigured by the temporal death of Aaron's sons.

10:2.t: And that He might increase in them this fear, immediately, by the mouth of offence, the rod of His chastisement was revealed, and after the offence the Chastiser gave them no respite, because their servitude was not worthy of His longsuffering. Above their head the rod of justice hung continually, and immediately they committed sin they were chastened, and at the time of their offence they were beaten, and at the entrance of the path of their sins they forthwith received rebuke; for longsuffering teacheth the foolish servant contempt, and in order that that stupid nation, which in the manner of an evil-doing servant, sat in the house of God, might not [learn] contempt, the Chastiser took away longsuffering, especially when they went forth from Egypt. […]
10:2.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 7 -- Second Discourse on the Fear of God

10:8.t: Let us see, then, what it is that has now been read to us. "And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: You shall drink no wine nor strong drink, you and your sons with you, when you enter into the tabernacle of testimony, or when you approach the altar, and you shall not die. This is a perpetual statute throughout your generations, to distinguish between the midst of the holy and the profaned, and between the midst of the unclean and the midst of the clean, and to instruct the children of Israel in all the statutes which the Lord has spoken to them by the hand of Moses". […]

If, then, we have understood what the inebriation of the saints is, and how this is given to the saints in the promises for gladness, let us now see how our Savior does not drink wine, "until he drink it new" with the saints "in the kingdom" of God. My Savior even now mourns my sins. My Savior cannot be glad, so long as I remain in iniquity. Why can he not? Because he himself is "the advocate for our sins with the Father", as John, his fellow-initiate, declares, saying that "even if anyone has sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just; and he is himself the propitiation for our sins". How, then, can he who is "the advocate for" my "sins" drink the wine of gladness, whom I sadden by sinning? […]

10:9.t: Priests given to wine are both condemned by the apostle and forbidden by the old law. Those who serve the altar, we are told, must drink neither wine nor shechar. Now every intoxicating drink is in Hebrew called shechar, whether it is made of corn or of the juice of apples, whether you distil from the honeycomb a rude kind of mead or make a liquor by squeezing dates or strain a thick syrup from a decoction of corn. Whatever intoxicates and disturbs the balance of the mind avoid as you would wine.

Gratuitous knowledge is called the knowledge of the Saints, because it has nothing of vice mixed in, nothing of carnality, nothing of curiosity, and nothing of vanity. Whence in Leviticus: "The Lord also said to Aaron: You and your sons shall not drink wine or anything that can intoxicate, so that you may have the knowledge of discerning between the holy and the profane." He who has the knowledge of discerning between the holy and the profane will abstain from everything that can intoxicate, that is, from every superfluous delight in creatures: this is the intoxicating wine. Whether someone on account of vanity, or on account of curiosity, or carnality inclines toward superfluous delight, which is in creatures: he does not have the knowledge of the Saints.

10:14.t: Scripture says, then: "the little breast of setting-apart and the arm of removal you shall eat in a holy place, you and your sons and your house with you; for it is given as a statute to you and a statute to your sons of the peace offerings of the children of Israel, the arm of removal and the little breast of setting-apart". Not every little breast is a "little breast of setting-apart", nor is every arm of "removal" or "separation" an "arm". But since we have recalled the person of the high priest to my Lord Jesus and to his sons the holy Apostles, let us see how he himself indeed eats the "little breast of setting-apart", and his sons, but the others cannot all eat the "little breast of setting-apart". […]

11:1.t: But now let us look also at some of those things which have been read concerning clean and unclean foods or animals; and just as in the explanation of the cup we ascended from the shadow to the truth of the spiritual cup, so also concerning the foods which are spoken of through the shadow, let us ascend to those which through the spirit are the true foods. But for investigating these things we have need of the testimonies of divine Scripture, lest anyone suppose—for men love "to sharpen their tongues like a sword"—lest anyone, I say, suppose that I do violence to the divine Scriptures and drag to men the things which are related in the law concerning animals, quadrupeds or even birds or fishes, clean or unclean, and feign that these were said concerning men. […]

But perhaps someone may say: concerning quadrupeds indeed and creeping things and birds you have rendered the reckoning, that men ought to be understood; give also concerning "those things which are in the waters". Since indeed the law designates concerning these too that some are clean and others unclean, I demand nothing in these matters, that my words be believed, unless I shall have given suitable witnesses. I will give you our very Lord and Savior Jesus Christ as witness and author of these things, how fishes are said to be men. "The kingdom of heaven is like", he says, "to a net cast into the sea, which gathers of every kind of fish; and when it has been filled, sitting upon the shore they store up those which are good in vessels; but those which are bad they cast forth". […]

11:3.t: With whom then should we live? With the just, he replies, again under a metaphor. Everything "of split hoof and chewing the cud" is clean, because the split hoof obviously is a sign of evenly balanced justice, which chews the cud of its own food of justice, the word, which enters from without through instruction. And, once within, [it] is recalled as if from the stomach of the mind for the musings of reason. The just man chews the cud of spiritual nourishment, because he holds the Word in his mouth. Justice undoubtedly divides the hoof, in that it both sanctifies in this life and prepares us as well for the life to come.

Therefore in the shadow of this meli tree the bride longs to abide — or the Church, as we said, in the protection of the Son of God, or the soul fleeing all the remaining doctrines and clinging to the one Word of God alone, whose sweet fruit she also has in her throat, that is, by meditating unceasingly on the law of God, and by always ruminating upon it like a clean animal.
11:3.s: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 3

11:3.t: "Every", it says, "beast that divides the hoof, and has hooves, and brings up rumination among the cattle, these you shall eat. Besides, of these you shall not eat, which bring up rumination, and do not divide the hooves, and have hooves. The camel, because it brings up rumination, and does not divide the hoof, this is unclean to you. And the hare, because it brings up rumination, and does not divide the hoof, this is unclean to you; and the hedgehog, because it brings up rumination, and does not divide the hoof, this is unclean to you; and the swine", and so forth. It decrees, then, that animals of this kind be not eaten, which in part seem to be clean and in part unclean; […]

For this reason it is also written in Leviticus: 'Every animal that divides the hoof and chews the cud is clean.' That is, if it has two hooves and chews the cud, it is clean. If therefore it has one hoof, it is not clean. The Jew has one hoof, and therefore is unclean. The Manichaean has one hoof, and therefore is unclean. And because it has one hoof, it does not chew over its food, and what it has once sent down into the belly it brings back up again to the throat, and chews it, and makes it fine, so that what had been coarse may be sent down again fine into the belly — this, indeed, pertains to the speaking of the divine mysteries. Every animal that divides the hoof and chews the cud is clean. […]

Hence it is properly decreed in the law that the only animals which are clean and suitable to be eaten by the people of God are those that have horns. For it is well known that those animals that chew the cud and divide the hoof are also those that have horns. So … it is mystically disclosed that the only people who can be incorporated into a spiritual union with the church of God are those who by the strength of their faith prove that they are unconquered in their battles with the vices.

11:7.t: The all-wise Educator, by the lips of Moses, compared association with corrupt men to living with swine when he forbade the ancient people to partake of swine. He made it plain in those words that they who invoke God should not seek the company of the unclean who, like swine, revel in bodily pleasures and filthy habits of life and impure delights, itching for evil-minded pleasures of sex.

It is then proper that the barbarian philosophy, on which it is our business to speak, should prophesy also obscurely and by symbols, as was evinced. Such are the injunctions of Moses: "These common things, the sow, the hawk, the eagle and the raven, are not to be eaten." For the sow is the emblem of voluptuous and unclean lust of food and lecherous and filthy licentiousness in venery, always prurient, and material, and lying in the mire and fattening for slaughter and destruction.

11:9.t: These things indeed have been said generally concerning animals; but those "which are in the waters", because they are said, if indeed they have "fins and scales", to be clean, but if they do not have them, unclean and not to be eaten: this is shown in them, that, if anyone is in these waters and set in the sea of this life and in the waves of the world, he ought nevertheless to strive earnestly not to lie in the depths of the waters, as are those fishes which are said "not to have fins nor scales". For this is reported to be their nature, that they always tarry in the lowest place and about the very mud; as are eels and things like this, which cannot ascend to the surface of the water nor reach its upper parts. […]

11:10.t: Hence again, fish that do not have fins are forbidden from being eaten by the faithful people. For fish that have scale-fins are also accustomed to leap above the waters. What therefore is figured by finned fish except elect souls? These alone indeed pass into the body of the heavenly Church, who, supported by the fins of virtues, know how to leap through heavenly desire, so that they may reach toward things above through contemplation, although they fall back again into themselves from mortal flesh.

11:13.t: He adds too that they are not to eat "kite or mastophage or eagle," meaning "You shall not go near those who make their livelihood by plundering others." He says other similar things under some sort of allegory.

And similarly concerning the birds. "You shall not eat", it says, "these, because they are unclean: the eagle and the vulture", and the rest like these. For to these birds the food is always of dead bodies, and they live from dead carcasses. All, then, who lead a life of this kind must be held unclean. I think that those too are numbered among these who brood over the deaths of others and by art or fraud forge testaments. For men of this kind will deservedly be called vultures and eagles, as gaping after the carcasses of the dead. I know also other flying things which live by rapine. These are the souls which, according to this indeed—that they are rational and imbued with liberal instruction or rational disciplines—seem to be flying things; […]

Now we say that the wicked are dead, but not in an ascetic life opposed to sin; nor do they, like the saints, bear about dying in their bodies. But it is the soul which they bury in sins and follies, drawing near to the dead, and satisfying it with dead nourishment; like young eagles which, from high places, fly upon the carcases of the dead, and which the law prohibited, commanding figuratively, ‘Thou shalt not eat the eagle, nor any other bird that feedeth on a dead carcase;’ and it pronounced unclean whatsoever eateth the dead.

11:44.t: "Be holy, says the Lord, for I am holy." The apostles boasted that they had left all things and had followed the Savior. We do not read that they left anything except their ship and their nets; yet they were crowned with the approval of him who was to be their judge. Why? Because in offering up themselves they had indeed left all that they had.

12:2.t: That our Lord Jesus Christ is called a physician in the divine Scriptures we are fully taught by the sentence of the Lord himself, as he says in the Gospels: "They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick. For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Now every physician compounds medicines beneficial to bodies from the juices of herbs or of trees, or even from the veins of metals or the natures of living creatures. But if someone should chance to look upon these herbs before they are compounded according to the reasoning of the art, then indeed, if they are in the fields or on the mountains, he tramples them underfoot and passes them by as worthless grass. […]

"And the Lord spoke," it says, "unto Moses, saying: Speak unto the children of Israel, and thou shalt say unto them: Whatsoever woman shall have conceived seed and borne a male, she shall be unclean seven days." First let us consider according to the history, whether it does not seem to be added as though superfluously: "the woman who shall have conceived seed and borne a male," as if she could bear a male otherwise than by seed conceived. But it is not added superfluously. For to distinguish her who "conceived and bore" without seed, the lawgiver added this word for the sake of the other women, so that he might designate as "unclean" not every woman who had borne, but her who "had borne with seed conceived." […]

Now, then, let us also inquire into this: what is the cause that a woman, who furnishes a ministry to those being born into this world, is said to be made "unclean" not only when "she has received seed," but also when "she has borne"? Whence also for her purification she is commanded to offer "young pigeons or turtledoves for sin at the door of the tabernacle of testimony," that "the priest may make propitiation for her," as one who owes a propitiation and a purification of sin for the fact that she furnished a ministry to a man being born into this world. For thus it is written: "And the priest shall make propitiation for her, and she shall be cleansed." […]

12:3.t: Which Sabbath He in His body abolished, although, nevertheless, He had formerly Himself commanded Moses that circumcision should not pass over the eighth day, which day very frequently happens on the Sabbath, as we read written in the Gospel.
12:3.s: On the Creation of the World

12:3.t: It was certainly not for nothing that the commandment was given for the child "to be circumcised on the eighth day"; it can only have been because the rock, the stone with which we are circumcised, was Christ. It was "with knives of rock" or stone that the people were circumcised;"now the rock was Christ." So why on the eighth day? Because in seven-day weeks the first is the same as the eighth; once you've completed the seven days, you are back at the first. The seventh is finished, the Lord is buried; we are back at the first, the Lord is raised up. The Lord's resurrection, you see, promised us an eternal day and consecrated for us the Lord's day. It's called the Lord's because it properly belongs to the Lord, because on it the Lord rose again. The rock has been restored to us; […]

12:6.t: But meanwhile she "who has borne a male," "on the eighth day" both the one who is born is circumcised and she is made clean. It is a matter of great labor for these things to happen in this brevity of time, yet, that we may say something in passing, this week may be seen as the time of the present life; for in a week of days the world was completed. In which, so long as we are set in the flesh, we cannot be pure to the point of clarity, unless the eighth day come, that is, unless the time of the age to come be present. On which day, however, he who is a male and has acted manfully is at once purified in the very coming of the age to come, and at once the mother who bore him is made clean; for she will receive the flesh purged of vices out of the resurrection. […]

12:8.t: The Lord commanded in the law that those who could were to offer a lamb for a son or a daughter, along with a turtledove or a pigeon. But one who did not have sufficient wealth to offer a lamb should offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons. Therefore the Lord, mindful in everything of our salvation, not only deigned for our sake to become a human being, though he was God, but also he deigned to become poor for us, though he was rich, so that by his poverty along with his humanity he might grant us to become sharers in his riches and his divinity.
12:8.s: HOMILY XV. ON THE PURIFICATION OF BLESSED MARY

13:2.t: We find, then, that six kinds are set forth concerning the leprosy of men, which six kinds are described in this manner. For either "in the skin of the body there comes a scar and a whitish sign in the skin of his body, the contagion of leprosy." Or "the leprosy flowering shall flower, and shall cover all the skin with the contagion from the head even to his feet." Or the third kind: "in the skin of the flesh there comes an ulcer and it is healed; and in the very place of the ulcer there comes a white scar." Or "in the skin of the flesh there comes a burning of fire, and" after these things "the healed burning shall be shining white, or bright with redness." The fifth kind, "when in a man or a woman there comes on the head or in the beard the contagion of leprosy." […]

13:12.t: But the second kind of leprosy is, if "it shall have flowered," it says, "in the skin, so that it covers all the skin of the body from the head even to the feet, throughout all things whatsoever the priest shall have inspected." When, then, it shall have covered over "all the skin of the body," then the priest pronounces him to be "clean" from the contagion. But "on whatsoever day there shall appear in him living color," again "he is judged unclean" through this, that "living color has appeared in him" which he did not have before. Concerning this some even before me have said that "living color" indicates the reason of life which is in man; […]

13:13.t: Thus he wished us to understand that the man who is changed from his former carnal state to the whiteness of faith (which the world considers a blemish and a stain) and who is completely renewed is clean. He is no longer spotted, no longer mottled with both the old and the new.

13:18.t: The third law concerning lepers is, "when in the skin of the body an ulcer is formed, and in the place of the ulcer a white scar with redness is found." But the cause of an ulcer is when in the body a filthy and noxious humor abounds. So then also in the soul are understood as ulcers those things which boil up from unclean desires or filthy thoughts. And if perchance these have been cured through the grace of faith and the remission of sins, and the soul has been made whole, nevertheless there remains "a scar," and that "scar" does not have a color like that of the body, but is "whiter," it is pronounced to be "leprosy." […]

13:24.t: The fourth was the law, where it is said that "if in the skin there comes a burning of fire," and after these things, "when the burning has been healed, it itself becomes shining and white with redness, or certainly whitish, and the appearance of it is lower than the rest of the skin": and this he says is "the leprosy which has flowered in the burning." See, then, whether "a burning" is not in every soul whatsoever that receives "the fiery darts of the evil one"; or whether everyone who burns in carnal love is not "scorched by fire." These, then, are the "burnings" and kindlings of "fire." But also he suffers "a burning" who is set ablaze by desire of human glory, and who is inflamed by the heats of anger or fury. […]

We read in Leviticus, if indeed we read with open eyes, and the veil that is placed upon the law does not shut out the gaze of the inner eye, that leprosy is wont to arise in the weal and scar of a burn, and to change the color of the hair, and that a new foulness is added to the former disfigurement of the scar. This is so for this reason: that no one, secure about repentance because after sin he can say: I will endure the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause, should sin and need cautery, and, once healed, be wounded again.

13:29.t: The fifth kind of leprosy is when "a contagion is formed on the head or in the beard of a man or a woman, so that the appearance of the contagion itself is lower than the skin of the body; and this is the leprosy of the head or of the beard." See, then, whether it can happen that "leprosy of the head" be thought to be in him who has not "Christ as his head," but some other — for example, Epicurus, who preaches pleasure as the highest good; does not both the head and the beard of such a man seem to you unclean? […]

13:40.t: Now the sixth and last kind of leprosy is set down, which "comes in baldness or forehead-baldness"; which things, as far as they are in themselves, are clean. For thus also the law says: "If any one's," it says, "hairs of the head have fallen off, he is bald, he is clean. But if they have fallen off from his forehead, he is forehead-bald, he is clean." And these things are suitably referred to the soul, so that, when it casts off and lays aside those things which are dead by their own nature, it is said to be clean. But after this, if those things which had first been purified shall be seen to sprout up again, filthier and lower than the dignity of purity requires, they will render the soul unclean and leprous.

13:45.t: From this now, generally, concerning every leper in whom there shall have been "the contagion of leprosy" and it shall appear "lower than the rest of the skin" — for every vice of the soul is lower than its remaining virtues — the law, which "is spiritual," decrees certain such things: "Let his garments," it says, "be unstitched, and his head uncovered, and his mouth covered over." By which it designates that he who is leprous in soul, that is, who is fixed fast with sins, ought not to sew coverings upon himself and to cover over the baseness of sin. For just as he whose "garments are unstitched" bears the baseness of his body naked and uncovered, so ought he who is hedged about with some sins to cover his evils and disgraceful deeds with no sewn-on words, with no veils of excuses; […]

13:46.t: "He shall be unclean," it says, "and shall sit separated outside, his dwelling shall be outside the camp." It is clear that every "unclean" one is cast out from the assembly of the good and separated from the company and camps of the saints; and therefore it says that: "his dwelling shall be outside the camp."

14:2.t: But if perchance he shall have been made clean, he does not indeed come of his own accord and by himself to the priest, but is offered, it says, by another, nor does he enter into the camp. For neither was it fitting that "on the same day on which he was made clean," before those things which were suitable were done for him, "he should enter into the camp." On account of which "the priest," it says, "shall go out to him outside the camp." For always to him who cannot yet "enter into the camp" there "goes out" that one who can "go out outside the camp," who says: "I went out from God and came into this world." "The priest goes out," then, "to him" and considers whether he now receives health, whether he is being purged from the contagion of leprosy.

And whoever will may see the profound and mighty mystery of Christ written for our benefit in Leviticus. For the law of Moses declares the leper defiled, and gives orders for him to be put out of the camp as unclean: but should the malady ever be alleviated, it commands that he should then be capable of readmission. Moreover it clearly specifies the manner in which he is to be pronounced clean, thus saying; "This is the law of the leper on whatsoever day he shall have been cleansed, and shall be brought unto the priest. And the priest shall go out of the camp, and the priest shall see him, and behold, the touch of the leprosy is healed from the leper: and the high priest shall command, and they shall take for him who is cleansed two living clean birds; […]
14:2.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

14:4.t: But when the priest shall have seen him, he commands that "there be taken two living hens for him who is being made clean, and cedar wood and twisted scarlet and hyssop." It seems to me that here too these "two hens" have a certain likeness of the two goats, of which one is offered to the Lord and the other is sent forth "into the wilderness"; for so here also, of the two hens, one is immolated and the other is let go "into the field." He, then, who is being purged of leprosy gives here too some part which is cast away "into the wilderness"; but the other part is offered to the Lord for him. Yet not yet does this one, who is being purged of leprosy and offers the hens, offer at the altar even that very hen which is offered for him to the Lord, as "turtledoves or doves." […]

Take for me a Jew reading Leviticus, and all those sacraments that are written there, and how the leper enters into the synagogue, how a hen is taken up, and its neck is wrung; then it is told how the blood is to be sprinkled, it is told of the water, it is told also of the hyssop, it is told too how his garments are to be rent, and thus he enters into the synagogue, he who had been a leper. If we read according to the letter, what profit is it to us that we read? But if we have turned to the heart, if we have understood spiritually, we shall see that the leper cannot enter to the people of God unless his garments be rent, unless whatever had been shut up be uncovered. Then see that this leper does not enter into the synagogue except through blood and water and hyssop. […]

The Lord also commanded Moses that if any leper were cleansed, he should come to the priest and offer two sparrows to the priest. Of these the priest, sacrificing one, should let its blood run down into living waters; and dipping the living sparrow into the waters into which he had made the blood of the sacrificed sparrow run down, together with cedar wood, scarlet wool, and hyssop, he should sprinkle the leper seven times, and then he would be duly cleansed (Lev. 14:1–7). By the priest Christ is understood; and by the two sparrows the teachers of the two Testaments are understood. […]

14:5.t: Yet observe also this, that the priest himself is not said to immolate the hen; for not yet is this one, who was a leper, worthy that the priest himself immolate for him. On account of which neither is the blood of the hen offered at the altar, but it says that "the hen shall be slain in an earthen vessel, in which vessel living water has been put," so that both water may be taken up for purification and the fullness of the mystery be completed in "water and blood," which is said "to have gone out from the side" of the Savior, and no less in what John sets down in his epistle and says, that purification is made "in water and blood and spirit." Whence here too I see all these things fulfilled. […]
